title: Diriyah: Birthplace of a Nation
summary: How Diriyah, beside Wadi Hanifah near Riyadh, became the capital of the first Saudi state in 1727, how its mud-brick town was built and later destroyed, and how it is restored and remembered on Founding Day.
poll: Restoring old towns like Diriyah is just as important as building new cities.

versions.title: Diriyah: Where It All Began
versions.text:
Near Riyadh is an old town. It is Diriyah. It is by a long valley. Palms grow there.

The town is old. It was built in 1446. It grew and grew. Then, in 1727, a man led it. His name was Muhammad bin Saud. He made it the capital of the first Saudi state. This is where our land got its start.

The homes were made of mud brick. The walls were thick. The sun was hot. But the rooms stayed cool. Small gaps let in air.

A big palace stood on a hill. It was in the main part of town. You can still see it.

The town was rich. Lots of folks came to trade. They sold dates. They sold goods.

In 1818, an army came. It broke a lot of the town. But that was not the end. Riyadh was the next capital.

Now the old town is fixed up. A visitor can walk its lanes. You can see the old homes. Each year, on 22 February, we mark Founding Day. We feel proud.

Diriyah has a long history. It was built in 1446, and over many years the small town grew larger. Then, in 1727, a leader named Imam Muhammad bin Saud made Diriyah the capital of the first Saudi state. For this reason, people call it the place where the nation began.

Diriyah became a busy and wealthy town. Traders came from near and far to buy and sell dates, cloth, and many other goods.

versions.title: Diriyah: Birthplace of a Nation
versions.text:
On the northwestern edge of Riyadh lies an old town called Diriyah. It stands beside Wadi Hanifah, a long valley where tall palm trees grow and where farms once stretched along the banks.

Diriyah has a long history. It was founded in 1446, and over the following centuries the small settlement grew larger. Then, in 1727, Imam Muhammad bin Saud made Diriyah the capital of the first Saudi state. For this reason, Saudis often describe it as the birthplace of their nation.

The houses of Diriyah were built from mud brick, a material made by mixing clay, straw, and water and drying it in the sun. The walls were very thick, which kept the rooms cool even under the fierce desert sun. Small openings near the tops of the walls allowed fresh air to circulate.

The grandest buildings stood on a hill in a district called At-Turaif. The largest of them, Salwa Palace, was where the rulers of the state lived and met. Visitors can still see the triangular openings and carved wooden doors that are typical of the traditional Najdi style.

Diriyah became a busy and wealthy town. Traders and travelers arrived from distant places to buy and sell dates, cloth, and many other goods.

In 1818, an invading army surrounded the town. After a long and difficult struggle, much of Diriyah was destroyed and abandoned. A few years later, Riyadh became the new capital.

Today, specialists have worked to restore the old town using traditional methods. In 2010, At-Turaif was named a World Heritage Site because of its importance to the history of the whole world. Every year on 22 February, Saudi Arabia celebrates Founding Day to remember the events of 1727.

versions.title: Diriyah: Birthplace of a Nation
versions.text:
On the northwestern edge of Riyadh lies a historic town called Diriyah. It stands beside Wadi Hanifah, a long valley where tall palm trees grow and where farms once stretched along the banks of a seasonal stream.

Diriyah has a remarkable history. It was founded in 1446 by Mani Al-Muraidi, an ancestor of the Al Saud family, and over the following centuries the modest settlement gradually expanded. Then, in 1727, Imam Muhammad bin Saud established Diriyah as the capital of the first Saudi state. For this reason, Saudis frequently describe it as the birthplace of their nation.

The town's architecture was well suited to the harsh climate. Houses were constructed from mud brick, a material produced by mixing clay, straw, and water and drying the mixture in the sun. Its walls were extremely thick, and this kept the interiors cool even under the fierce desert sun, while small triangular openings near the tops of the walls provided ventilation.

The most impressive buildings stood on a hill in a district called At-Turaif. The largest, Salwa Palace, served as the residence and meeting place of the rulers. Visitors can still admire the decorated wooden doors that are characteristic of the traditional Najdi style.

Diriyah developed into a busy and prosperous town, attracting merchants and travelers from distant regions who came to trade dates, cloth, and many other goods.

In 1818, forces sent by the Ottoman governor of Egypt placed the town under siege. After several months of exhausting struggle, much of Diriyah was destroyed and abandoned. A few years later, Riyadh became the capital of the second Saudi state.

The story of the nation continued long afterward. In 1902, King Abdulaziz regained Riyadh, and in 1932 he united the regions under his rule as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

Today, specialists have restored the old town using traditional building methods. In 2010, UNESCO declared At-Turaif a World Heritage Site because of its importance to the shared history of humanity. Since 2022, Saudi Arabia has celebrated Founding Day every year on 22 February to commemorate the events of 1727.

versions.title: Diriyah: Birthplace of a Nation
versions.text:
On the northwestern outskirts of Riyadh lies a historic town called Diriyah, which stands beside Wadi Hanifah, an elongated valley where tall palm trees flourish and where cultivated farms once stretched along the banks of a seasonal stream.

Diriyah possesses a remarkable history. It was founded in 1446 by Mani Al-Muraidi, an ancestor of the Al Saud family, and over the following centuries the modest settlement gradually expanded. Subsequently, in 1727, Imam Muhammad bin Saud established Diriyah as the capital of the first Saudi state, which explains why Saudis frequently describe it as the birthplace of their nation.

The town's architecture was ingeniously adapted to the unforgiving climate. Residences were constructed from mud brick, a material produced by combining clay, straw, and water and drying the mixture in the sun. The walls were exceptionally thick, which kept the interiors comfortably cool even beneath the fierce desert sun, while small triangular openings near the tops of the walls provided ventilation.

The most impressive structures occupied a hill in a district called At-Turaif. The largest, Salwa Palace, functioned as both the residence and the administrative center of the rulers. Visitors can still admire the decorated wooden doors and geometric patterns that are characteristic of the traditional Najdi style.

Diriyah developed into an energetic and prosperous town, attracting merchants and travelers from distant regions who arrived to exchange dates, textiles, and numerous other commodities.

In 1818, military forces dispatched by the Ottoman governor of Egypt placed the town under siege. After several months of exhausting resistance, much of Diriyah was destroyed and abandoned. Within a few years, however, Riyadh had become the capital of the second Saudi state.

The narrative of the nation continued well beyond these events. In 1902, King Abdulaziz regained control of Riyadh, and after three decades of determined effort, he unified the regions under his authority in 1932, proclaiming the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the third and current Saudi state.

In recent decades, specialists have meticulously restored the old town using traditional construction techniques. In 2010, UNESCO designated At-Turaif a World Heritage Site in recognition of its significance to the shared history of humanity. Since 2022, Saudi Arabia has celebrated Founding Day annually on 22 February to commemorate the events of 1727. The surrounding area now also contains museums, galleries, and restaurants that welcome thousands of visitors.

versions.text:
On the northwestern outskirts of Riyadh lies a historic town called Diriyah, which stands beside Wadi Hanifah, an elongated valley where tall palm trees flourish and where cultivated farms once stretched along the banks of a seasonal stream.

Diriyah possesses a remarkable history. It was founded in 1446 by Mani Al-Muraidi, an ancestor of the Al Saud family, and throughout the following centuries the modest settlement gradually expanded. Subsequently, in 1727, Imam Muhammad bin Saud established Diriyah as the capital of the first Saudi state, which explains why Saudis frequently characterize it as the birthplace of their nation.

The town's architecture was ingeniously adapted to the unforgiving climate. Residences were constructed from mud brick, a material produced by combining clay, straw, and water and drying the mixture in the sun. The walls were exceptionally thick, which kept the interiors comfortably cool even beneath the fierce desert sun, while small triangular openings positioned near the tops of the walls provided essential ventilation.

The most impressive structures occupied an elevated plateau in a district called At-Turaif, and the largest of them, Salwa Palace, functioned simultaneously as the residence and the administrative headquarters of the rulers. Visitors can still admire the decorated wooden doors and intricate geometric patterns that are characteristic of the traditional Najdi style.

Diriyah developed into an energetic and prosperous community, attracting merchants and travelers from distant regions who arrived to exchange dates, textiles, and numerous other commodities.

In 1818, military forces dispatched by the Ottoman governor of Egypt placed the town under siege. After several months of exhausting resistance, much of Diriyah was destroyed and subsequently abandoned. Within a few years, however, Riyadh had become the capital of the second Saudi state, demonstrating that the political community founded in Diriyah had survived the destruction of its original capital.

The narrative of the nation continued well beyond these events. In 1902, King Abdulaziz regained control of Riyadh, and after three decades of determined military and diplomatic effort, he unified the regions under his authority in 1932, proclaiming the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the third and current Saudi state.

In recent decades, specialists have meticulously restored the old town using traditional construction techniques. In 2010, UNESCO designated At-Turaif a World Heritage Site in recognition of its significance to the shared history of humanity. HIGH.prompt: Some people say that the past should be preserved, while others say money should go to new projects. Using evidence from the article, explain why restoring Diriyah was worthwhile.
checklist: I stated a clear position about restoring Diriyah.
I supported it with at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
I used precise vocabulary, including at least two key words.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I believe restoring Diriyah was worthwhile. First, the town's mud-brick architecture shows clever ventilation, since small openings near the tops of the thick walls let fresh air flow through and kept rooms cool in the desert heat, a heritage worth preserving. Second, Diriyah survived a serious siege in 1818 and was nearly destroyed, so restoring it honors the people who once lived and traded there as a prosperous town. Third, being named a World Heritage Site in 2010 shows that the whole world values this history, and the yearly Founding Day celebration helps commemorate the moment the first Saudi state began.
